title: How conveyor-belt sushi (kaiten-zushi) was invented in Osaka, 1947–1978

sources.publisher: Organization for Small & Medium Enterprises and Regional Innovation, JAPAN (J-Net21)

facts.text: Yoshiaki Shiraishi moved to Osaka in 1947 and ran a restaurant in Fuse (now part of Higashiosaka) where customers ate sushi standing up.
His standing sushi bar sold sushi more cheaply than other shops and was always crowded.
The work was hard, so his young workers kept quitting and he was always short of staff.
Shiraishi got the idea after seeing beer bottles carried on a conveyor belt at a beer factory (an Asahi brewery in Suita, Osaka).
He thought a conveyor belt would let him run the shop with fewer workers and lower the cost of sushi.
Building the machine took years; the hardest problem was the corners, where plates fell off the belt.
He solved the corner problem with fan-shaped pieces, an idea that came from children spreading playing cards in a fan; local small factories helped build the belt.
The first conveyor-belt sushi restaurant, Mawaru Genroku Sushi, opened in April 1958 near Kintetsu Fuse Station in Higashiosaka.
A Genroku restaurant at the 1970 Osaka world's fair (Expo '70) was very popular, with long lines, and made conveyor-belt sushi famous across Japan.
The Expo restaurant stood near the American and Soviet pavilions, so many foreign visitors ate there.
Shiraishi's patent on the conveyor table ended in 1978; after that, other companies could open conveyor-belt sushi restaurants, and many new chains appeared.
The invention turned sushi, once thought of as a luxury, into an everyday food that ordinary people could afford.
Japan now has more than 4,000 conveyor-belt sushi restaurants.
